title: The Cron That Grew

scenario.situation: The nightly data pipeline is a chain of 30 cron jobs on a single VM. When one fails midway, the team finds out from broken morning reports and reruns everything by hand. The lead proposes building a custom scheduler on Kubernetes.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The lead believes the fix is a bespoke Kubernetes-based scheduler the team builds in-house.
scenario.question: What's the real gap in the cron setup, and what's the right-sized way to close it?

decisions.prompt: How do you approach the fix?

options.label: Start building the custom Kubernetes scheduler
options.detail: Begin implementing the in-house orchestrator the lead proposed.
options.consequence: You begin writing a bespoke orchestrator — retries, DAG state, backfills, a UI — reinventing a solved problem before you've even named which capabilities you actually need.
options.divergenceCost: Started building a scheduler before specifying which orchestration capabilities are missing.

options.label: Enumerate what's actually failing about cron
options.detail: List the concrete gaps: dependencies, retries, visibility, backfills.
options.consequence: You list the real gaps: no dependency awareness (jobs fire on a clock, not on upstream success), no automatic retries, no run visibility, and painful manual backfills. These are exactly the problems a workflow orchestrator solves.

options.label: Wrap the existing crons in more error-handling shell
options.detail: Add retry loops and alerting scripts around the current jobs.
options.consequence: You bolt retry loops and alerts onto brittle bash; it helps a little, but dependency ordering and backfills are still manual, and you've grown the very tangle you meant to escape.
options.divergenceCost: Patched the symptoms in shell instead of addressing the missing orchestration model.

options.label: Move the crons onto a bigger, more reliable VM
options.detail: Assume the machine is the weak point and upgrade it.
options.consequence: A beefier VM does nothing — the failures aren't about the machine, they're about the lack of dependency-aware scheduling and recovery.
options.divergenceCost: Treated an orchestration-reliability gap as a hardware problem.

decisions.prompt: You've named the gaps. How do you decide between building a scheduler and adopting one?

artifact.title: The four gaps — who provides them?

options.label: Compare on how much control a custom build gives you
options.detail: Weigh the flexibility of owning every line of the scheduler.
options.consequence: A bespoke scheduler would give total control — and total ownership of retries, state, UI, and every future edge case, forever. You'd be maintaining infrastructure that isn't your product.
options.divergenceCost: Weighed control while ignoring the permanent maintenance cost of owning undifferentiated infrastructure.

options.label: Compare capability coverage and total maintenance cost of adopt vs build
options.detail: Ask which option closes all four gaps, in what time, and who maintains it afterwards.
options.consequence: A managed orchestrator (e.g. Airflow / Cloud Composer) covers all four gaps out of the box in days, versus months to build and years to maintain a custom one. Orchestration is undifferentiated heavy lifting — nothing about it is specific to your business. Adopt wins decisively.

artifact.title: Adopt vs build — effort and ownership

options.label: Recommend building the custom scheduler for maximum flexibility
options.detail: Own the orchestrator so you can tailor every behavior.
options.consequence: The team signs up to build and forever maintain a general-purpose orchestrator — undifferentiated work that competes with actual data delivery for engineering time. Flexibility you'll rarely use, paid for continuously.
options.divergenceCost: Recommended owning undifferentiated infrastructure for flexibility the team is unlikely to need.

options.label: Adopt a managed orchestrator, note the lock-in tradeoff, migrate incrementally
options.detail: Propose an existing orchestrator, acknowledge the tradeoff, and move the crons over in stages.
options.consequence: You propose adopting an existing orchestrator that closes all four gaps, acknowledge the tradeoff (some framework lock-in and a learning curve), and plan an incremental migration so nothing breaks at once. The team gets reliability in weeks and keeps its time for work that's actually theirs.

insight: Cron's failures weren't about the machine or missing error-handling — they were the absence of an orchestration model: dependency-aware scheduling, automatic retries, backfills, and run visibility. Every one of those is standard in an existing orchestrator, so building a bespoke Kubernetes scheduler would have re-implemented — and then permanently maintained — a solved, undifferentiated problem. The lesson is to separate the capabilities you genuinely need from the instinct to build: adopt commodity infrastructure and reserve engineering for what's actually specific to your business.
